text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

❓ Core Question/Dilemma
Can the High Court quash GST show-cause notices and adjudication orders on limitation grounds when an effective statutory appeal is available and the dispute involves disputed questions of fact?
🔹 The Verdict
The Delhi High Court relegated the Assessee to the statutory appellate remedy, leaving the limitation disputes open for examination by the Appellate Authority.

🔹 The Dispute
• The Assessee challenged GST adjudication proceedings for FY 2017–18 and another GST order, alleging that the relevant show-cause notices and adjudication orders were time-barred.
• The Department disputed the limitation claims, relying on its stated dates of issuance and email communication of the notices and orders.

🔹 The Legal Basis
• Section 74(9) and Section 74(10), CGST Act, 2017: The Assessee relied on the statutory limitation provisions governing adjudication, while the Department disputed the allegation of delay.
• Section 14, Limitation Act, 1963: The Appellate Authority was directed to consider, in accordance with law, any request for exclusion of the period during which the writ petitions remained pending.

An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

"Section 6 of the MWP Act."

Under Indian debt recovery laws, a standard nominee is merely a trustee.

If you pass away with an active loan, lenders have the legal right to claim your insurance money to clear your unpaid debt before your family gets a single rupee.

Friend X bought a regular policy with his wife as nominee.
(The bank legally seized the payout against his home loan).

Friend Y ticked one free box during application: "Policy under MWP Act."

That single checkbox turns the policy into an irrevocable trust.
It stops being part of your personal estate. Banks, recovery agents, and civil courts have ZERO legal power to touch that money.

100% of the claim goes strictly to the wife and kids.

The only rule: You must select it while buying the policy. You cannot convert an existing policy later.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

IBC में छूटा GST Claim… अब नहीं चलेगा!
IBC Plan Approved. ₹1.85 Crore Demand Quashed.

● ● ●

⭐ आज की बात

नमस्ते दोस्त!

ज़रा सोचिए…

एक कंपनी मुश्किल दौर से गुज़री। मामला Insolvency तक पहुँचा।

फिर एक Resolution Plan बना। NCLT ने उसे approve कर दिया और कंपनी नए Management के साथ आगे बढ़ने लगी।

लेकिन कहानी यहीं खत्म नहीं हुई!

करीब दो साल बाद पुराने GST का मामला फिर सामने आ गया।

Department ने लगभग ₹1.85 Crore की Demand खड़ी कर दी।

अब सवाल था…

जिस पुराने GST Claim को Insolvency Process में उठाया ही नहीं गया, क्या उसे बाद में Notice भेजकर दोबारा ज़िंदा किया जा सकता है?

यही मामला पहुँचा Calcutta High Court।

● ● ●

⭐ कहानी में असली मोड़ कहाँ आया?

मामला SREI Equipment Finance Limited का था।

Department का आरोप था कि कंपनी ने FY 2021-22 में imported goods पर ₹1.68 Crore का excess IGST ITC लिया था।

इसके साथ ₹16.87 Lakh की Penalty और Interest भी लगाया गया।

लेकिन इस Demand के पीछे एक महत्वपूर्ण तारीख छिपी थी।

कंपनी का CIRP 8 October 2021 को शुरू हुआ था।

11 August 2023 को NCLT ने Resolution Plan approve कर दिया।

और सबसे महत्वपूर्ण बात?

GST Department ने इन पुराने dues का Claim CIRP में lodge ही नहीं किया था।

फिर भी September 2025 में SCN आया और December 2025 में Demand confirm कर दी गई।

● ● ●

⭐ कंपनी और Department की दलील क्या थी?

कंपनी ने कहा कि Resolution Plan approve होने के बाद पुराने, unclaimed GST dues खत्म हो चुके थे।

Department की दलील थोड़ी अलग थी।

उसके अनुसार Tax Liability तय करना और उसकी Recovery करना दो अलग बातें हैं।

भले Recovery नहीं हो सके, लेकिन Tax Demand determine की जा सकती है।

अब Court को इसी अंतर पर फैसला करना था।

● ● ●

⭐ Court ने कौन-सी बात पकड़ ली?

🔍 Calcutta High Court ने सबसे पहले देखा कि GST Claim किस period का था।

FY 2021-22 की पूरी अवधि Resolution Plan approve होने से पहले की थी।

और उस Claim को Insolvency Process में पेश भी नहीं किया गया था।

इसलिए Court ने माना कि वह Claim 11 August 2023 को ही extinguish हो गया था।

फिर Court के सामने एक सीधा सवाल आया।

जब Claim ही कानूनन खत्म हो चुका है, तो उसके आधार पर नई GST Proceeding कैसे शुरू हो सकती है?

● ● ●

⭐ इस Judgment का Crux Point

यह मामला सिर्फ GST Recovery रोकने का नहीं था।

Court ने स्पष्ट किया कि जब कोई पुराना Claim approved Resolution Plan के बाद extinguish हो चुका हो, तो उस Claim पर नई Adjudication भी नहीं की जा सकती।

यानी Department का यह तर्क स्वीकार नहीं हुआ कि Recovery भले रुके, लेकिन Demand तय करने की Proceeding चल सकती है।

● ● ●

⭐ Judgment में किन Legal References का इस्तेमाल हुआ?

📂 IBC Section 31(1) के अनुसार approved Resolution Plan Government Authorities पर भी binding होता है।

Section 238 IBC को conflicting कानून पर overriding effect देता है।

📚 Supreme Court के Ghanashyam Mishra और Essar Steel judgments से Court ने यह principle लागू किया कि successful Resolution Applicant को पुराने, अनसुलझे Claims के नए बोझ के बिना business आगे बढ़ाने का अवसर मिलना चाहिए।

📚 Department ने Sundaresh Bhatt judgment का सहारा लिया। लेकिन Court ने बताया कि वह Moratorium और Liquidation से जुड़ी अलग स्थिति थी।

📂 Court ने CBIC Circular 134/04/2020-GST और Instruction 1083/02/2022-CX8 का भी उल्लेख किया, जो Insolvency Claims के treatment को recognize करते हैं।

● ● ●

⭐ आखिर इस कहानी का नतीजा क्या निकला?

✅ Calcutta High Court ने 26 September 2025 का GST SCN और 29 December 2025 का Demand Order quash कर दिया।

DRC-01, DRC-07 और उनसे जुड़ी Proceedings भी set aside कर दी गईं।

July–August 2021 के delayed GSTR-3B filing से संबंधित अलग Section 50 Interest Notice भी quash हुआ।

लेकिन एक बात समझना जरूरी है।

⚠️ Court ने यह तय नहीं किया कि विवादित ITC वास्तव में सही था या गलत।

और बाद की किसी अलग Tax Liability, यदि हो, उस पर भी कोई फैसला नहीं दिया।

● ● ●

⭐ चलते चलते

इस फैसले से Business Owners और GST Professionals के लिए एक महत्वपूर्ण सीख निकलती है।

अगर किसी कंपनी का Resolution Plan approve हो चुका है और उसके बाद पुराने GST Period का Notice आता है, तो केवल Demand Amount मत देखिए।

तीन सवाल जरूर पूछिए:

1️⃣ Tax किस period का है?

2️⃣ Resolution Plan कब approve हुआ?

3️⃣ क्या Department ने CIRP में उस Claim को lodge किया था?

क्योंकि कभी-कभी GST Notice का जवाब केवल GST Records में नहीं, बल्कि कंपनी के Insolvency Records में छिपा होता है।

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

text:
2020: AT1 bonds written off. 2023: Bombay HC says no. 2026: Supreme Court agrees. What a journey.

The Yes Bank AT1 bond story is one of the most interesting chapters in Indian banking and investing.

Here is what happened:

→ March 2020: Yes Bank was placed under a moratorium. Withdrawals were restricted to ₹50,000, with limited exceptions allowing up to ₹5 lakh for specified emergencies.

→ The moratorium was supposed to run until April 3, but the reconstruction happened quickly and the new board took charge on March 26.

→ As part of the rescue, ₹8,415 crore of Yes Bank AT1 bonds were written down to zero. AT1 bonds are not normal FDs or ordinary bonds. They are designed to absorb losses when a bank gets into serious trouble.

→ The problem was that many retail investors claimed they had been mis-sold these AT1 bonds as something similar to an FD.

SEBI's investigation records complaints where investors said relationship managers told them the bonds were safer than FDs, or even persuaded them to break an FD and invest in AT1 bonds.

→ There was another controversial chapter involving the erstwhile Reliance Mutual Fund, now Nippon India Mutual Fund.

SEBI later investigated investments made during the Reliance Capital era. The regulator alleged a possible quid pro quoinvolving Yes Bank's lending to Reliance Group companies. The amounts and allegations have evolved through different regulatory and investigative proceedings, so this should not be treated as a finally established finding against every person involved.

→ In 2023, the Bombay High Court quashed the AT1 write-off, holding that the administrator did not have the required authority under the final reconstruction scheme to wipe out the bonds.

→ Yes Bank, RBI and the Government challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.

→ And today, 15 October 2026, the Supreme Court dismissed those appeals and upheld the Bombay High Court judgment. The ₹8,415 crore write-off has therefore been held legally invalid.

So what does this mean?

A big day for AT1 bondholders.

Especially for investors who were genuinely mis-sold these instruments as “safe”.

A difficult day for Yes Bank.

The bank now faces the consequences of a judgment that restores the bondholders' claims.

And an interesting development for SMBC.

Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation acquired 20% of Yes Bank in 2025 and subsequently increased its holding, with RBI approval for up to 24.99%.

And yes, Nippon India MF investors who were affected by the AT1 write-off also stand to benefit from the court ruling, subject to how the judgment is implemented and the amounts ultimately recoverable.

The biggest lesson for investors?

“Bond” does not mean “safe”.

And a product being sold by a bank relationship manager does not make it an FD.

AT1 bonds were created precisely because they can absorb losses when a bank gets into trouble.

This case also shows something else:
Courts can sometimes change an outcome that risk managers, regulators and investors thought was already settled.

Earlier today, @Meta temporarily removed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's video on the NEET paper leaks in India. According to media reports, a Meta spokesperson stated that the post was taken down due to an error and it had since been restored, post-haste.

The temporary removal of PM Modi's post highlights the larger issue of wrongful content takedowns by these platforms, often without any notice to users and leaving them with no meaningful recourse. These takedowns may be carried out by automated systems that have  been deployed as part of the growing due diligence obligations under Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, or by way of government-issued order which reflects as a “legal request” on the platform.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has seen multiple instances of automated monitoring systems wrongfully taking down content, with no available recourse but engaging with the platform's internal appeals mechanisms and grievance officers. While high profile instances such as this are resolved quickly, ordinary users are often left high and dry. These issues are exacerbated by the lack of human review in the escalation process, with aggrieved users facing constant automated and AI generated responses which often fail to address even the most apparent errors in moderation. Coupled with unresponsive and inefficient grievance officer reporting procedures, users are all but helpless. Platforms may deploy these automated systems to deal with the huge volumes of content that they have to moderate under the existing regulatory system, especially since many of these obligations are tied to the safe harbour provisions under the IT Act that exempt platforms from being liable for the content they host. However, having humans in the loop for grievance redressal would ensure that fair outcomes are delivered to all and not only to high-profile persons.

According to media reports, the Delhi Police has also identified around 450 social media accounts that allegedly shared deepfakes and AI generated content related to the protests. The Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove this kind of content shared during the CJP protests, along with other content considered "objectionable" that relates to the Prime Minister.

Such vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” are inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding the reasons for these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where various government and law enforcement bodies decide the limits of free speech without transparency or oversight. An illustrative example is the temporary restriction faced by the @Cockroachisback’s primary Instagram handle, which was entirely blocked  on the evening of July 22. As per media reports, the account was restored after the Union Government reversed the blocking and advised the law enforcement agency that “action should be limited to specific posts or URLs instead of the entire account.”

It is not just the Prime Minister’s  post or CJP’s account that has faced such removals recently. Under the decentralised and opaque content removal regime, dozens of Instagram posts and videos related to the protests have been taken down, either by automated systems or in response to government orders, and many users have even had their accounts restricted. For these users, without high-profile attention, regaining access to their accounts or having the content restored is a long and arduous process, with no guarantee of remedy or reprieve.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

PAYAL GAMING DEEPFAKE CASE: HOW CYBER POLICE HELPED RESTORE HER REPUTATION

Police traced the accused and authenticated the video as a deepfake, providing a certificate to the creator.

A crucial step in establishing the truth, countering misinformation and helping restore a victim’s reputation.

Deepfakes can damage reputations. Timely investigation and digital evidence can help fight back.

SEM order (NDTV, DNA): one SURETY couldn't give Das's parentage/address; the other had an Aadhaar photo mismatch.

DOJ Charges 28 Green-Card Holders In California Noncitizen-Voting Sweep (Oct. 19)

Federal prosecutors charged 28 lawful permanent residents in California with illegally registering to vote. Prosecutors allege 21 of them cast ballots, some in multiple elections. Eleven were arrested Monday and 17 more are expected to be taken into custody. Charges include fraudulent registration and, for some, false statements on naturalization paperwork. All 28 appear on a list of about 20,000 “likely noncitizen” registrants that DOJ gave California officials last week. DOJ has also sued the state to block counting mail ballots from people on that list until citizenship is confirmed. Officials say 113 people in 20 states have been charged in recent weeks. State and county officials had not responded at the time of reporting, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

Source: Washington Examiner; Washington Times; Associated Press

Kansas Man Charged With Threatening Trump Ahead Of Wichita Rally

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Kansas filed a complaint
Oct. 17 against Jaden J. Read, 24, of Clearwater, under the federal statute on threats against the president. The charge carries up to five years in prison. A Crime Stoppers tip led investigators to Facebook comments on local news stories about the president’s visit. Prosecutors allege the posts called for shooting Trump and claimed Read had mapped nearby rooftops. He remains in federal custody pending a detention hearing. Trump was scheduled to rally Monday evening for Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tightening race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Separately, Mediaite reported that Secret Service Director Sean Curran told “60 Minutes” on Sunday that threats against protectees are up about 40%.

Source: U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Kansas; KSN; Washington Examiner; NBC News; Mediaite

Trump And Vance Hit The Trail In The Midterm Homestretch

Election Day is Nov. 3. Trump’s week includes Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa and Florida, with Georgia and Michigan next weekend. Vance campaigned in Hendersonville, N.C., on Monday and announces a Nebraska stop Thursday. In North Carolina he announced an additional $858 million in Transportation Department disaster funds for Hurricane Helene recovery. Early voting opened Monday in Texas. Gray DC, citing the latest race ratings, says Democrats hold an edge in the fight for Congress. CNBC reported Sunday that Democrats are surging in fundraising while Elon Musk backs Republicans.

Source: Washington Examiner; Gray DC; CNBC

DOJ Opens Civil-Rights Probe Into D.C. Jails (Oct. 19)

Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon notified Mayor Muriel Bowser that DOJ will investigate whether the D.C. Department of Corrections engages in a “pattern or practice” of violating inmates’ constitutional rights. The review covers safety, living conditions and meals. This is the opening of an investigation, not a finding of wrongdoing.

Source: Washington Examiner

INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS  🌐

Lavrov Visits Tehran; No New Russian Mediation Plan Announced (Oct. 19)

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met Iran’s Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian. It was his first Iran visit since the U.S.-Israeli war began Feb. 28. He called the strikes illegal and urged a return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz. In Bahrain earlier, he urged both sides to revisit the Pakistan-brokered Islamabad memorandum. That agreement collapsed within weeks after Iran attacked ships it said were violating it. The New Arab reported that neither side announced a new mediation initiative. Araghchi blamed the U.S. war and its naval blockade for the insecurity. He said Iran’s seven-day ceasefire and phased-reopening offer is still on the table. The offer requires the U.S. to lift the blockade and sanctions, and Trump rejected it last month. Washington says the Strait is open to everyone except Iran and wants nuclear issues addressed at the outset.

Source: Washington Times; CBS News/AP; The New Arab; Fox News

Trump Endorses Netanyahu Ahead Of Oct. 27 Israeli Vote (Oct. 18–19)

Trump gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a full endorsement Sunday. He said that if Israel chooses a different leader, the U.S. would have to handle Iran largely alone. He also said the U.S. could soon complete the effort against Iran unless Tehran changes course. On Monday Netanyahu posted video of a phone call with Trump in which he said, “we have a job to finish.” Netanyahu has said he told Israeli security agencies to work toward toppling the Iranian regime. Araghchi dared the U.S. to strike again and accused Netanyahu of pushing America into war to avoid prosecution. That is an Iranian claim.

Source: Fox News; CBS News

Trump Waives Russia Sanctions; Gop Senators Object (Order Signed Oct. 16)

Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act. The law, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was signed Sept. 18 and was due to take effect two days later. Trump certified to Congress that the waiver serves the national interest. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration will take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called it “a carrot” to end the war and said Russia currently exports no diesel. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis, John Cornyn and Kevin Cramer and Rep. Don Bacon criticized the move. Democrats including Chuck Schumer also attacked it. CBS reports the roughly 300,000-ton Russian diesel purchase is about 2.2 million barrels, only a bit over half of one day’s U.S. diesel use. It also notes that delivery timing is unclear because Ukraine has damaged Russian refining capacity.

Source: CBS News; Reuters via Fox News; TheStreet

Trump–Zelenskyy Rift Deepens; Putin Floats Trump–Xi Summit; Starlink Questions Persist (Oct. 19)

Trump said Monday that Ukraine should pick “somebody else” to negotiate, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump is on the wrong side of history. Per the Wall Street Journal, Putin proposed a Trump–Xi–Putin summit without Zelenskyy during an Oct. 9 call. The idea could tie in with November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Rubio said a meeting has been discussed but is not finalized. Zelenskyy says throttled Starlink/Starshield speeds are hampering drone interception. Musk says Starshield limits are set by the U.S. government and ultimately the president. Trump denied imposing them and said Monday he did not know who ordered them but wants to find out. Nine senators have asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate. Tillis and Sen. Richard Blumenthal said after a Monday call that Zelenskyy reported disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing. HuffPost reported Rubio says sharing never stopped.

Source: Washington Examiner; CBS News; Wall Street Journal via TheStreet; HuffPost

France: Arrests Top 2,000 After Violent Cost-Of-Living Protests (Oct. 17–18)

France’s Interior Ministry reported 2,397 arrests Saturday and 997 police and gendarmes injured. Authorities put turnout at about 550,000 and organizers at about 800,000. Macron expressed “anger and shame” in a televised address, promised rioters would pay for their crimes, and vowed “full transparency” on the police response after criticism of inadequate preparation. Trump posted “France is burning!” and appeared to link the unrest to immigration. Vance also blamed immigration. French authorities have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have pointed to “radical far-left groups” and opportunistic looters. Oil Swings On The Russia Waiver And Houthi Attacks; Pump Prices Ease Slightly

Brent settled Friday at $109.86, its highest since May 19. Crude dipped early Monday after the Russia waiver. WTI then reversed to about $103.73 by mid-afternoon, up roughly 2.4%, after Houthi attacks on Saudi targets. AAA’s national gasoline average was $4.30 Monday, down from $4.36 a week earlier. AAA says this is the first October above $4. Diesel hit a record near $6.49 in September. Wright said gasoline never approached $5 and is falling. Homebuilder Sentiment Hits Lowest Since 2012

The NAHB/Wells Fargo index fell three points to 29, below the 31 economists expected. Freddie Mac says the 30-year mortgage averaged 7.40% last week, a near three-year high. Builders cited energy-linked costs, tariffs and labor shortages. Forty-three percent cut prices. NAHB chairman Bill Owens said more than one-third of builders reported immigration-enforcement activity in their areas that delayed projects and discouraged legal workers from showing up.

Source: Reuters via TheStreet

Saudi Investor Forum Postponed To 2027 (Oct. 19)

Organizers moved the Future Investment Initiative from Oct. 26–29 in Riyadh to 2027 amid Houthi attacks. The postponement follows a reported Oct. 10 attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed at least 12. Scheduled speakers included top Wall Street CEOs.

Trump Signs Women’s Health Order Creating Nih Division And Task Force (Oct. 19)

The order establishes a Women’s Health Division at NIH and a White House task force led by Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and HHS Secretary Robert F. A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

text:
IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

This video is said to be from 2009. Look at how the Election Commission of India functioned then, and compare it with what is happening today.

The Election Commission freely encouraged citizens to exercise their voting rights. Its advertisements highlighted the problems people faced in everyday life, including corruption, poor education, inadequate healthcare, crumbling infrastructure and bad governance, and reminded them that the power to change these conditions lay in their votes.

The central purpose was to promote universal adult franchise, encourage electoral participation and increase voter turnout.

Watch this advertisement carefully. It clearly conveys the message that if the government has failed to deliver good governance, the citizens have the power to change it through elections.

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

India reserves every right under the Constitution to defend its news narrative — Just like how France, Germany, USA and many other democratic countries always do.

Sovereignty is not protected only at the border. It is protected in the newsroom.

For the last ten days, watch the reporting playbook. BBC, Associated Press, Reuters are running the same tweaked script on India. A fringe protest of 150 people by the Cockroach Janata Party at Connaught Place becomes "India's GenZ uprising." A preventive arrest under BNSS Sections 126 and 170, produced before Special Executive Magistrate at Mandir Marg, becomes "crackdown on democracy." A lawful order under Section 163 BNSS to protect Rajiv Chowk traders becomes "curfew-like ban on dissent."

The double standard is visible when you compare Paris and Delhi this week. In Paris, 5.5 lakh people marched, 1,200 to 1,800 were arrested, 150 policemen injured, a 140-year-old town hall in Limoges was largely destroyed, the tourist office in Lyon was torched, shops looted from Marseille to Bordeaux. French media and international agencies called it "cost of living protest" and "police maintain order" even when tear gas and water cannons were fired.

In Delhi, police did not fire a single tear gas shell, did not use water cannons, did not fire rubber bullets. No shop was looted, no building burned. Fourteen people trying to breach de-notified Jantar Mantar were detained and later released on a Rs 50,000 peace bond. Same agencies called it "India stifles dissent."

This is narrative warfare, not news.

Every democracy acts against it. India should also do it. Nothing new.

France passed two anti-fake news laws in 2018. Under that law, a judge can order immediate removal of inaccurate or misleading allegations during elections when disseminated massively in a deliberate, artificial manner, and the broadcast regulator CSA can prevent, suspend or prohibit a foreign TV service that harms fundamental interests of the nation by disseminating false information. Violation carries one year imprisonment and 75,000 Euro fine. 

Germany passed NetzDG, penalising platforms up to 50 million Euros for not removing false narratives. Singapore's POFMA allows fines up to S$1 million and 10 years jail for falsehoods. The US uses FARA to register and monitor foreign-funded media influence. UK's Ofcom can revoke licences for biased or harmful coverage.

Why should India be apologetic for protecting its own? Why?

When the BBC ran a one-sided documentary on India, when AP uses unnamed sources on sensitive election issues, when Reuters crops a 150-person protest to look like a mass movement, these are not mistakes. They feed global rankings, feed opposition press conferences, and feed foreign funding justifications.

Let's be absolutely clear. Article 19(1)(a) gives press freedom, Article 19(2) puts reasonable restrictions for sovereignty, security and public order. Controlling false news is not censorship of truth. It is the duty of the government and all other stakeholders including citizens, under the Constitution of India. 

Indian government must do everything... use the latest of latest technologies including AI-based tracking of tweaked narratives, enforce fact-check units, demand right of reply, require transparency of foreign funding behind news portals, and enforce BNSS provisions against deliberate falsehood. Like France has a special judge to delete fake news in 48 hours, India too should have fast-track judicial orders for removal of proven false anti-India narratives instantly. The courts of law must strongly support within the framework of the Constitution.

Protecting India's story is protecting India's democracy. It is the primary responsibility and duty of the legislature, the executive, the judiciary and the national media too. 

And, it must be done 24X7 all through the year at all times.

On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of.
